nodes.label: Company Knowledge Base
nodes.desc: The single place every agent reads from and writes to. Not software you buy · plain files with a strict convention: who the company is, what it sells, how it speaks, what is true right now. An agent with this context writes like a colleague. An agent without it writes like a stranger.
nodes.replaces: Re-briefing every tool, agency, hire, and AI session from scratch, forever. The context tax is invisible because everyone pays it · until one company stops paying it and starts compounding instead.

ladder.manual: Context lives in the founder’s head and a thousand chat threads. Every new session starts at zero.
ladder.assisted: Core files exist · company, offer, voice, per-client state · and humans update them after meaningful work.
ladder.autonomous: Every transcript, email, and deliverable writes itself back. Any agent or human reads one page and is current. The brain maintains the brain.

nodes.notes: Build this before anything else on the map · every department’s first node assumes it exists. It is one session of work: scaffold the files, get interviewed, install the read-before-write rules. The test that it works: a smart stranger could read the folder and act for you tomorrow. The skill below does the entire setup.
nodes.human: Everyone writes to it, one human owns it · usually the founder, eventually an ops lead. Ownership of the brain is the last job that never automates.

nodes.label: Sales
nodes.subtitle: targeting · outreach · sequencing
nodes.description: The top of the funnel · finding the right companies, learning enough about them to be worth a reply, and reaching out at scale without sounding like a robot. This is the department most businesses try to hire their way out of. It is the one agents change first, because every job here is research, writing, and timing · and machines never get tired of any of it.

nodes.label: ICP Definition
nodes.description: Define and refine ideal customer profiles per vertical · firmographics, pain patterns, buying triggers.

playbook.human: The founder owns this forever. AI drafts and refreshes; the human decides who the business is for. Never fully delegated.
playbook.replaces: The founder’s gut feel, applied inconsistently by everyone downstream. Bad ICP wastes every dollar spent after it.

ladder.manual: A slide from 2 years ago that nobody opens.
ladder.assisted: AI drafts ICP profiles per vertical from your closed-won data; a human edits quarterly.
ladder.autonomous: Profiles update themselves as deals close and lose · win patterns feed back in without a meeting.

playbook.notes: Start here. This is the first node of the Sales tree for a reason · every job downstream (sourcing, scoring, writing) reads from it. Write one page per vertical: firmographics, the pain in the buyer’s words, the trigger that makes them buy now. Store it where your agents can read it, not in a deck.

nodes.label: Market Mapping
nodes.description: Map the total addressable companies in a target vertical before a campaign.

playbook.replaces: Guessing how big the pond is. Teams campaign into verticals without knowing whether the addressable universe is 400 companies or 40,000 · and misprice the effort either way.

ladder.manual: A spreadsheet of companies somebody had heard of.
ladder.assisted: The agent builds the full universe per ICP · every company that fits, counted and segmented · and a human sanity-checks the edges.
ladder.autonomous: The map refreshes as companies get founded, funded, and folded; campaign planning reads live numbers, not last year’s guess.

playbook.notes: This is TAM at the company-name level, not the analyst-report level · a list you can actually campaign into. Know the denominator before you spend: a 4,000-company vertical justifies a system, a 150-company vertical justifies a hand-written letter each. The trap is mapping by industry code · SIC and NAICS lie constantly. Map by what companies actually do, scraped from what they say about themselves.

nodes.label: Trigger Detection
nodes.description: Watch for buying signals · hiring, funding, tech changes, leadership moves.

playbook.replaces: Outreach timed by your calendar instead of theirs. The gap between a 2% and a 10% reply rate is often just catching a company the week something changed.

ladder.manual: You see the funding announcement on LinkedIn three weeks after everyone else did.
ladder.assisted: Watched accounts get scanned for hiring spikes, funding, tech changes, and leadership moves; flagged leads land with the trigger attached.
ladder.autonomous: A trigger fires and the lead enters the right sequence the same day, with the trigger written into the opener.

playbook.notes: A detected signal nobody references is a wasted signal · the trigger has to reach the first line of the email, not sit in a CRM field. Start with the two or three triggers that genuinely map to your offer (hiring an SDR team if you sell outbound, a new ops lead if you sell automation) and ignore the rest. The trap is watching everything: ten signal types produce noise, two produce openers.

nodes.label: Lookalike Modeling
nodes.description: Build new target lists off the shape of your closed-won accounts.

playbook.replaces: The expansion list nobody builds methodically · most teams guess at "who else looks like our best clients" instead of extracting the actual pattern.

ladder.manual: Someone eyeballs the closed-won list and says "let’s target more companies like these."
ladder.assisted: The agent extracts the real shared firmographics + triggers from closed-won, builds a lookalike query, and hands back a ranked new list.
ladder.autonomous: Every close feeds the model · the lookalike list refreshes itself and flows straight into sourcing.

playbook.notes: This is ICP Definition pointed backwards · instead of who you think you want, it reads who actually bought and finds more of them. The quality depends entirely on having clean closed-won data, so it sits downstream of Win/Loss Analysis.

nodes.label: Database Mining
nodes.description: Pull targeted company and contact lists from structured databases.

playbook.human: A human sets the target and spot-checks 10 rows per pull. Bad lists poison everything downstream · the check takes five minutes and saves a campaign.
playbook.replaces: 4–6 hours/week of an SDR pulling and cleaning lists · roughly $8–12k/year of a $65k rep’s time spent not selling.

ladder.manual: Someone exports CSVs from a database tool and fixes them in spreadsheets.
ladder.assisted: You describe the target in plain language; the agent builds the query, pulls, dedupes, and hands back a clean segmented list.
ladder.autonomous: Standing searches run weekly per ICP; new matches land pre-scored, with verified contacts, with no one asking.

playbook.notes: The skill below builds tiered lead lists from structured databases and the open web, and degrades gracefully based on which API keys you have. Feed it your ICP file · the output quality is a direct function of node one.

nodes.label: Web & Maps Scraping
nodes.description: Scrape local businesses, directories, and niche sources for leads.

playbook.replaces: The lists databases don’t sell · local businesses, niche directories, marketplaces. Built by hand this is days of copy-paste per territory, so it simply doesn’t get built.

ladder.manual: Copy-pasting business names out of Google Maps into a spreadsheet at 1am.
ladder.assisted: Point the agent at a geography and a category; it scrapes, structures, dedupes against past pulls, and hands back clean rows.
ladder.autonomous: Standing scrapes per territory refresh on schedule; new openings show up in your pipeline before competitors know they exist.

playbook.notes: This is where local and SMB lists live · the big databases are weakest exactly where Maps and directories are strongest. Scraped data is also the dirtiest data you’ll touch: route everything through verification before it gets near a sequence. The trap is one giant pull and done · territories change monthly, and the refresh is where the edge is.

nodes.label: Social Mining
nodes.description: Harvest engaged audiences · post commenters, followers, group members.

playbook.replaces: The list nobody builds by hand: everyone who engaged with a competitor’s post is a warm prospect, but scraping them manually takes hours per post.

ladder.manual: You screenshot commenters and look them up one by one.
ladder.assisted: Point the agent at a post or profile; it harvests engagers, enriches, scores against ICP, and drafts the first DM.
ladder.autonomous: Watched accounts and keywords feed a standing warm-prospect pool, refreshed continuously.

playbook.notes: Highest-intent cold list you can build · these people already raised their hand on the topic. The skill below scrapes engagers, enriches profiles, ICP-scores, and writes openers in one pass.

nodes.label: List Building
nodes.description: Merge, dedupe, and segment raw leads into campaign-ready lists.

playbook.replaces: The 2–3 hours per campaign of merging CSVs and fighting duplicates · and the reputational cost when the same CEO gets the same email from two of your sequences.

ladder.manual: VLOOKUP, tears, and the same person in three rows under slightly different spellings.
ladder.assisted: Raw pulls from every source merge, dedupe, and segment into named campaign lists on command.
ladder.autonomous: Every sourcing job feeds one canonical pool; campaign lists assemble themselves with suppression · clients, open deals, past bounces · applied automatically.

playbook.notes: The suppression list is the underrated half of this job: nothing torches trust like cold-emailing a current client or an open deal. Keep one canonical lead pool that every campaign draws from, not per-campaign spreadsheets that drift apart. The trap is deduping on email alone · dedupe on person and company, or the same prospect with two addresses slips through twice.

nodes.label: Contact Enrichment
nodes.description: Find and append emails, phones, and LinkedIn profiles to every lead.

playbook.replaces: A list you can’t reach. Without enrichment, 40–60% of a raw list has no usable contact · paying for leads and reaching half of them is the silent tax on every campaign.

ladder.manual: Guessing first.last@company.com and hoping.
ladder.assisted: Waterfall enrichment runs per lead · email, direct dial, LinkedIn · across multiple providers, appended to the record.
ladder.autonomous: Every lead entering the pool enriches on arrival; coverage rates and cost-per-found-contact tracked per provider.

playbook.notes: Waterfall is the whole pattern: no single provider covers more than ~70%, so chain two or three and take the first valid hit. Track cost-per-found-contact by provider and cut the losers quarterly. The trap is enriching before filtering · paying to find the phone number of a lead you were never going to contact. Score and segment first, enrich what survives.

nodes.label: Email Verification
nodes.description: Validate every address before it ever gets a send.

playbook.replaces: Domain burn. A 5% bounce rate doesn’t cost you 5% of sends · it gets the domain flagged, and the next 10,000 emails land in spam.

ladder.manual: Send and find out.
ladder.assisted: Every address passes through a verifier before it touches a sequence; catch-alls and risky addresses get flagged for a decision.
ladder.autonomous: Verification runs on the way in and re-runs on any list older than 90 days; anything under threshold never reaches a sender.

playbook.notes: This is a gate, not a feature · nothing unverified gets sent, ever, and bounce rate stays under 2%. Decide your catch-all policy explicitly: send to them on a separate domain or don’t send at all, but never mix them into your clean volume. The trap is verifying once and trusting forever · addresses decay 2–3% a month as people change jobs.

nodes.label: Account Enrichment
nodes.description: Layer firmographics, tech stack, and headcount trends onto target accounts.

playbook.replaces: The research step everyone skips: outreach to a company you don’t understand reads like spam because it is.

ladder.manual: A glance at the website before the call.
ladder.assisted: Tech stack, headcount trends, and growth signals appended to every target account on demand.
ladder.autonomous: Accounts re-enrich on a schedule; material changes (funding, hiring spikes, stack changes) trigger alerts to the targeting layer.

playbook.notes: Pairs with Company Deep-Dive in the Intelligence department · enrichment is the bulk pass, deep-dive is the surgical one for accounts worth a real pursuit.

nodes.label: Fit Scoring
nodes.description: Score every lead against ICP so outreach spends effort where it converts.

playbook.replaces: Reps spending identical effort on a perfect-fit account and a tire-kicker, because the list doesn’t know the difference. Effort allocation is the multiplier on everything downstream.

ladder.manual: Sort by company size and call it prioritization.
ladder.assisted: Every lead scores against the ICP file · firmographics, tech stack, triggers · and lands in a tier before any send.
ladder.autonomous: Scores recompute as enrichment refreshes; A-tier routes to high-touch sequences, C-tier to low-cost ones, without anyone deciding per lead.

playbook.notes: A score that doesn’t change behavior is decoration · each tier must get genuinely different treatment: sequence depth, personalization effort, channel mix. Calibrate against closed-won quarterly: if your last ten wins weren’t A-tier, the model is wrong, not the wins. The trap is the 100-point model nobody trusts · three tiers with legible rules beat it every time.

nodes.label: Personalization Research
nodes.description: Build a personalization dossier per prospect · hooks, context, common ground.

playbook.replaces: 10–15 minutes per prospect done properly · which is why nobody does it properly past the first twenty.

ladder.manual: Two minutes on LinkedIn, then “Love what you’re doing at {company}!”
ladder.assisted: The agent builds a dossier per prospect · hooks, recent moves, common ground · and a human picks the angle.
ladder.autonomous: Every lead that enters a sequence carries its dossier with it; the writer agents consume it directly.

playbook.notes: This is the difference between personalization and mail-merge. The skill below produces a structured dossier per person: what they’ve said publicly, what changed at their company, and the two strongest hooks to open with.

nodes.label: Cold Email Drafting
nodes.description: Write multi-step cold email sequences tuned to the vertical and offer.

playbook.human: A human approves every new sequence before launch and owns the offer it sells. Once a sequence is proven, AI varies it within the approved frame.
playbook.replaces: A $60–80k/year SDR’s core output · or a $2–4k/month agency retainer that sends the same template to everyone.

ladder.manual: One template, first-name token, pray.
ladder.assisted: The agent writes the full sequence per segment from your offer doc and dossiers; a human approves before launch.
ladder.autonomous: Sequences generate per campaign, A/B variants included, with reply data feeding the next round’s angles.

playbook.notes: Voice is the whole game. The skill below reads your offer and tone files before it writes a word · set those up first or you’ll get competent generic. Three-step sequences, problem → proof → door-close. Never lead with price.

nodes.label: LinkedIn Messaging
nodes.description: Draft connection notes and DM sequences that read human.

playbook.human: Messages send under a real person’s name · that person reads what goes out under it. Approval per sequence, not per message.
playbook.replaces: The 30 connection requests/day a founder sends in a good week and zero in a busy one. Consistency is the entire channel.

ladder.manual: Copy-pasted “I’d love to connect” notes.
ladder.assisted: Connection notes and DM sequences drafted per prospect from their dossier; human sends.
ladder.autonomous: Sequenced sending through an outreach platform, with replies routed back into the pipeline automatically.

playbook.notes: Shorter than email, more human, no links in the first message. The skill below drafts the full connection → DM → follow-up arc and exports to sending platforms.

nodes.label: Proof Matching
nodes.description: Match the right case study to each prospect’s industry and problem.

playbook.replaces: Sending the SaaS case study to the manufacturer. Generic proof reads like no proof · relevance is what makes evidence land, and matching it by hand is one more step nobody does at volume.

ladder.manual: The same two logos in every email, regardless of who’s reading.
ladder.assisted: The agent picks the closest-match case study per prospect · industry, problem, company size · and writes the one-line proof into the draft.
ladder.autonomous: Every sequence pulls its proof at generation time; a new case study enters the library and immediately starts appearing wherever it fits.

playbook.notes: The library structure is the actual work: every case study tagged by vertical, problem, and outcome, each with one quotable number. A near-match in their industry beats a bigger number from a different world · buyers pattern-match on “that’s me” before they read the result. The trap is letting the agent round numbers up for effect: proof goes out verbatim or not at all.

nodes.label: Cold-Call Scripting
nodes.description: Call and voicemail scripts with branching objection handling that read human.

playbook.replaces: The reps who freeze on the call because nobody wrote the branches · or the "script" that’s one paragraph and dies at the first objection.

ladder.manual: A rep improvises, or reads a stiff script that the prospect can hear is a script.
ladder.assisted: The agent writes the opener, the pattern interrupt, the value line, and a full objection-branch tree with example phrasing for each.
ladder.autonomous: Scripts regenerate per segment as objection data comes back from real calls.

playbook.human: A human delivers it · this drafts the words, the rep makes them sound like a person. The objection branches are the value, not the opener.
playbook.notes: The skill below writes call + voicemail scripts that read human, with branches for "not interested", "send me an email", "we already have someone", "no budget". Feed it the offer and one real objection and it tightens fast.

nodes.label: Video Prospecting
nodes.description: Personalized video scripts · the hook, the personal line, the CTA, under 90 seconds.

playbook.replaces: 10+ minutes per personalized video done right · which is why reps record three then quit.

ladder.manual: A rep stares at a Loom recording light with no script and rambles for two minutes.
ladder.assisted: The agent writes a sub-90-second script · on-screen hook, a first line about the prospect’s actual world, one value beat, one CTA.
ladder.autonomous: Every lead in a sequence carries a personalized video script generated from its dossier.

playbook.notes: Video works because almost nobody does it well, and it dies because almost nobody scripts it. The skill below scripts the hook + personal line + value + CTA from the prospect dossier · the human just hits record.

nodes.label: Campaign Orchestration
nodes.description: Build multi-channel cadences · email, LinkedIn, phone touches in order.

playbook.replaces: Single-channel outbound. Email-only gets email-only results · coordinated email, LinkedIn, and phone touches lift reply rates 2–3×, but sequencing them by hand across hundreds of leads is a planning job nobody sustains.

ladder.manual: An email sequence here, some connection requests there, and no relationship between them.
ladder.assisted: The agent assembles the full cadence · which channel, which day, which message · from your drafted assets; a human approves the plan.
ladder.autonomous: Cadences build per segment from the playbook; the channel mix adjusts itself based on what actually got replies last quarter.

playbook.notes: The channels have to know about each other: the LinkedIn note lands after email two and references the thread · or references nothing if it went unanswered. Map the whole arc before the first send; retrofitting coordination onto a live campaign is misery. The trap is believing more touches means more replies · 8–12 touches over three weeks, then stop and hand the silence to Reactivation.

nodes.label: Campaign Launch
nodes.description: Push finished campaigns into sending platforms with correct settings.

playbook.human: A human reviews the rendered test send before volume flows. Launch is the last gate where a broken token costs nothing · one minute of eyes here versus 2,000 apologies later.
playbook.replaces: The hour of fiddly platform setup per campaign · and the occasional disaster where the {firstName} token goes out raw to the whole list.

ladder.manual: Copy-paste the sequence into the sender, set the limits from memory, hope.
ladder.assisted: Finished campaigns push into the sending platform with schedules, limits, custom fields, and tracking configured; a human checks the test send.
ladder.autonomous: Approved campaigns deploy themselves · settings pulled from the playbook, test send auto-rendered and checked, go-live logged.

playbook.notes: Turn the launch checklist into code: daily limits set, tracking domain live, custom fields mapped, unsubscribe working, test send rendered and read. The render check catches the embarrassing failure class · broken personalization tokens · before anyone outside sees it. The trap is launching to the full list at once: ramp over days, both for deliverability and so a bad sequence dies at 10% sent instead of 100%.

nodes.label: Deliverability
nodes.description: Keep domains healthy · warmup, spam testing, inbox rotation.

playbook.replaces: The silent campaign killer. Everything upstream can be perfect and none of it matters from spam · and most teams find out a month of wasted sends too late.

ladder.manual: Reply rates fall off a cliff and somebody eventually wonders why.
ladder.assisted: Inbox placement tests, warmup, and domain health checks run on schedule; problems surface with the fix attached.
ladder.autonomous: Rotation, warmup, and volume throttling self-manage; a domain showing strain gets pulled from rotation before it burns.

playbook.notes: Architecture first: cold volume goes through secondary domains, never your main one · 2–3 inboxes per domain, 30–50 sends per inbox per day, warmed for 2–3 weeks before real volume. From there it’s monitoring: placement tests and bounce trends on a schedule, not when things feel slow. The trap is treating this as one-time setup · deliverability is a tide, not a switch, and it only moves one direction unattended.

nodes.label: Send Optimization
nodes.description: Schedule sends by timezone and pace volume to protect reply rates.

playbook.replaces: Blasting everyone at 9am your time · including the prospects for whom that’s 2am, and the inbox providers for whom that spike looks exactly like spam.

ladder.manual: Send-all, then refresh the dashboard.
ladder.assisted: Sends schedule per recipient timezone and pace inside provider-safe volume; the agent proposes window changes from reply data.
ladder.autonomous: Send timing tunes itself per segment from observed reply patterns; volume flexes up and down with domain health.

playbook.notes: Timezone correctness alone is worth real points of reply rate · a 9am email read at 9am is a different email than one buried under the overnight pile. Pacing should look human: spread through the working day, randomized intervals, no perfect cron-job spikes. The trap is over-tuning send windows on small samples · you need hundreds of sends per cell before timing data means anything; until then, recipient-morning and move on.

nodes.label: Deals
nodes.subtitle: replies · calls · closing · pipeline
nodes.description: What happens after someone raises their hand · the reply gets read and routed, the meeting gets booked, the proposal gets written, the pipeline stays honest. Speed wins deals here, and speed is exactly what a human team loses as volume grows. The agents answer in minutes, draft before the next call, and never let a deal go quiet without flagging it.

nodes.label: Reply Classification
nodes.description: Read every reply and tag it · interested, objection, referral, not now, never.

playbook.human: Edge cases route to a human within minutes; everything else is logged for a weekly 15-minute audit of the classifier’s calls.
playbook.replaces: The inbox-checking anxiety loop. At volume, a human misses hot replies for 6+ hours · and speed-to-reply is the highest-leverage variable in outbound.

ladder.manual: Founder reads every reply, usually at midnight.
ladder.assisted: Every reply auto-tagged · interested / objection / referral / not-now / never · with drafted responses queued for approval.
ladder.autonomous: Interested replies route to the calendar in minutes; objections get library responses; only edge cases reach a human.

playbook.notes: The pattern that scales outbound past one inbox. Build the objection library from your real replies · after ~50 classified threads the categories stabilize and the drafts stop needing edits. This is the node franchise networks and multi-territory businesses feel hardest.

nodes.label: Objection Response
nodes.description: Draft responses to common objections from a tuned library.

playbook.human: The library is human-authored from real won deals · AI retrieves and adapts, it never invents a new counter-argument that no one has tested live.
playbook.replaces: Re-improvising the same five rebuttals forever. Every outbound motion gets the same objections · price, timing, “we have someone”, “send info” · and most reps answer each one slightly worse than last time.

ladder.manual: You retype your best comeback from memory, slightly different every time, usually softer.
ladder.assisted: Each classified objection gets a drafted response from a tuned library · your strongest past answer, adapted to this thread · queued for approval.
ladder.autonomous: Known objections get library responses on send-approval autopilot; novel objections route to a human and their winning answer joins the library.

playbook.notes: Build the library from threads you actually won, not from sales books · your real replies beat generic frameworks. Five objections cover 80% of volume; write one great answer per objection per offer and stop there. The trap is over-arguing: the best objection responses concede something true, then reframe in one short paragraph.

nodes.label: Hot-Lead Routing
nodes.description: Route interested replies to the calendar and the pipeline instantly.

playbook.replaces: The hours an interested reply sits in an inbox while the prospect cools. Interest decays by the hour · a hot reply answered next morning converts at a fraction of one answered in minutes.

ladder.manual: The hot reply is item 47 in the inbox and gets the same priority as the newsletter.
ladder.assisted: Interested replies get flagged, pushed to the deal owner, and pre-loaded with a booking-ready response in minutes.
ladder.autonomous: Hot replies skip the queue entirely · calendar link sent, deal created at the right stage, owner notified, all before a human has read the thread.

playbook.notes: This is plumbing, not intelligence · the classifier already found the gold; routing just refuses to let it sit. Wire it to the calendar and the CRM in the same motion so a hot reply becomes a booked slot and a pipeline record, not a notification. The trap is routing on weak signals: tune the classifier conservative, because one fake-hot alert per day teaches the owner to ignore all of them.

nodes.label: Meeting Booking
nodes.description: Propose slots, book calls, chase no-shows.

playbook.human: The calendar owner sets the rules once · buffers, hours, who qualifies. The agent never negotiates exceptions; humans do.
playbook.replaces: The 4–7 message back-and-forth that kills deal momentum, plus the no-shows nobody chases.

ladder.manual: “What times work for you?” × 3.
ladder.assisted: Agent proposes slots from the live calendar and books on confirmation.
ladder.autonomous: Hot replies get slots in the first response; no-shows get a recovery sequence automatically.

playbook.notes: Wire it to your real availability with buffers, not your aspirational one. The no-show recovery sequence alone pays for the build · most teams just let those die.

nodes.label: Referral Capture
nodes.description: Spot the "talk to my colleague" replies and action the warm intro.

playbook.replaces: The warm intros that evaporate · a prospect says "talk to my colleague in ops" and the reply sits unactioned for a week until the moment’s gone.

ladder.manual: A rep reads the reply, means to follow up on the referral, forgets.
ladder.assisted: The agent flags every "talk to / loop in / not me but" reply, drafts the warm-intro ask, and routes the new contact into the pipeline.
ladder.autonomous: Referral replies are detected, the intro is drafted, and the new lead is created and assigned without a human touching the inbox.

playbook.notes: Referrals close roughly twice as fast as cold · and they’re the leakiest part of most pipelines because they arrive as a throwaway line in a reply. This catches them the moment they land.

nodes.label: Speed-to-Lead
nodes.description: Acknowledge and engage every inbound lead within minutes.

playbook.replaces: The two days between a form fill and a founder’s reply. Inbound leads contacted within five minutes convert at multiples of those contacted next-day · and most businesses are measured in days.

ladder.manual: The lead fills the form Tuesday, hears back Thursday, signed with someone else Wednesday.
ladder.assisted: Every inbound lead gets an acknowledgment within minutes · personal in tone, specific to what they asked · with the human looped in for the real conversation.
ladder.autonomous: First response, qualifying question, and booking link fire inside five minutes around the clock; the human wakes up to scheduled calls, not raw form fills.

playbook.notes: The first message only has two jobs: prove a human-quality brain read their submission, and open the next step. Reference what they actually wrote · a reply that mirrors their form answer beats any template. The trap is sounding like an autoresponder; if the message could have been sent without reading the submission, rewrite the system.

nodes.label: Lead Qualification
nodes.description: Parse intake forms and score inbound leads before a human looks.

playbook.human: AI scores and sorts; a human owns where the disqualification line sits and audits the auto-declines. Spotting the bad-fit lead that’s secretly a strategic exception stays a judgment call.
playbook.replaces: 30–45 minutes of discovery call per lead that should never have been booked. Unqualified calls are the most expensive way to learn someone has no budget.

ladder.manual: Everyone who books gets a call; you find out they’re a student with a question at minute four.
ladder.assisted: Intake answers parsed and scored against your ICP · budget, fit, urgency · with a recommended route (book, nurture, decline) before a human looks.
ladder.autonomous: Qualified leads book straight onto the calendar, marginal ones enter a nurture track, and poor fits get a polite redirect · no human triage at all.

playbook.notes: The intake form is the real build: ask three questions that predict close · budget range, problem in their words, timeline · and the scoring becomes trivial. Score against your closed-won pattern, not an aspirational ICP. The trap is over-filtering early: log every auto-declined lead and audit the list monthly until you trust the line.

nodes.label: Comment-CTA Fulfillment
nodes.description: Detect keyword comments on content and deliver the promised asset by DM.

playbook.replaces: Manually DMing a link to 400 commenters · which means either hours of phone time after every post that pops, or broken promises to the exact people who raised their hands.

ladder.manual: You send the first 30 DMs by thumb, lose steam, and the other 370 commenters get nothing.
ladder.assisted: Keyword comments detected per post; the promised asset goes out by DM from a queue a human can watch.
ladder.autonomous: Every comment-CTA post fulfills itself · keyword detected, asset delivered, email captured, lead tagged by which asset they wanted · at any volume, at any hour.

playbook.notes: This is the bridge between content and pipeline: the comment is a hand-raise, the DM is the capture, the asset is the excuse. Gate the asset behind an email and the content engine starts feeding the CRM directly. The trap is stopping at delivery · tag every lead with which asset they claimed, because that tag is targeting data for everything downstream.

nodes.label: Inbox Triage
nodes.description: Sort inbound email and DMs · client, lead, brand deal, noise.

playbook.replaces: The founder as a human sorting machine · 60–90 minutes a day deciding what each message even is before any real work starts, with the important ones buried under the noise.

ladder.manual: Everything is unread, everything is urgent, the client email from Tuesday surfaces Friday.
ladder.assisted: Every inbound email and DM tagged on arrival · client, lead, brand deal, admin, noise · with the must-answer items surfaced first.
ladder.autonomous: The inbox sorts itself continuously; noise never reaches a human, leads route to the pipeline, client messages flag the right project, and you work a ranked queue instead of a timeline.

playbook.notes: Triage is classification plus routing · the tag is worthless unless something happens because of it: leads to the pipeline, client items to the project context, noise to archive. Start with five categories maximum; precision beats granularity. The trap is silent misfiling · keep a weekly audit of what got tagged noise, because one mis-archived client email costs more than the system saves.

nodes.label: Pre-Call Briefing
nodes.description: Build a brief before every call · who, company, history, objectives, talking points.

playbook.replaces: The 20 scrambled minutes before every call · or worse, walking in cold and asking questions the website answers.

ladder.manual: Skim their LinkedIn in the waiting room.
ladder.assisted: A one-page brief lands before every call: who, company, history, last conversation, open threads, suggested objectives.
ladder.autonomous: Briefs generate from the calendar automatically · every external meeting, no trigger needed.

playbook.notes: Reads the CRM, past transcripts, and email threads. The compounding effect is real: by call three the brief knows more about the relationship than you remember.

nodes.label: Call Capture
nodes.description: Record, transcribe, and file every meeting automatically.

playbook.human: Humans run the meeting; the system just never forgets it. Flag sensitive calls as do-not-record · the convention matters more than the tool.
playbook.replaces: Notes that don’t exist, decisions nobody wrote down, and “wait, what did we agree?”

ladder.manual: Pen, paper, vibes.
ladder.assisted: Every meeting recorded and transcribed via a notetaker; transcripts filed per client.
ladder.autonomous: Transcripts flow into the knowledge base automatically and become readable context for every other agent.

playbook.notes: The single cheapest high-leverage node on this map · a notetaker subscription and a filing convention. Everything in the Deals and Operations trees gets smarter the day this turns on. If you deploy one node this month, deploy this one.

nodes.label: Post-Call Debrief
nodes.description: Extract outcomes, action items, and deal updates from the transcript.

playbook.human: The deal owner skims the extracted actions same-day · 2 minutes to confirm what a human promised another human.
playbook.replaces: 30 minutes of post-call admin per meeting that either eats selling time or doesn’t happen.

ladder.manual: Action items live in your head until they don’t.
ladder.assisted: Transcript → outcomes, action items, deal-stage updates, drafted within minutes of hang-up.
ladder.autonomous: CRM updates itself, tasks assign themselves, and the follow-up email is waiting in drafts.

playbook.notes: Combine with Follow-Up Drafting: the recap email should arrive while the prospect still remembers the call. Same-day follow-up measurably outperforms next-day · and AI makes same-hour trivial.

nodes.label: Follow-Up Drafting
nodes.description: Draft the recap email with next steps before the prospect forgets the call.

playbook.replaces: The recap email that goes out two days late or never. Deals lose momentum in the gap between the call and the follow-up · and the gap is usually just the seller being busy.

ladder.manual: You mean to send the recap tonight; tonight becomes Thursday; Thursday becomes “following up on our chat last week”.
ladder.assisted: The recap drafts itself from the transcript within minutes of hang-up · what was agreed, next steps, owners · waiting in drafts for a read and a send.
ladder.autonomous: Every external call produces its follow-up automatically; the human edits the occasional nuance, and same-hour recaps become the house standard.

playbook.notes: Speed is the feature: a same-hour recap lands while the prospect still feels the call, and it quietly sets the version of events on your terms. Keep it short · decisions, next steps with owners and dates, one forward-looking line. The trap is sending a transcript summary instead of a sales document; the recap should advance the deal, not minute the meeting.

nodes.label: Objection Library
nodes.description: Mine every call for the objections that come up · build the rebuttals that win.

playbook.replaces: The objection-handling knowledge that lives only in the head of your best closer · and walks out the door when they do.

ladder.manual: Every rep relearns the same objections from scratch, badly.
ladder.assisted: The agent mines every recorded call for objections, clusters them, and drafts the rebuttal that actually moved deals forward.
ladder.autonomous: The library updates itself as new calls land · new objections surface, weak rebuttals get flagged and rewritten.

playbook.notes: This turns your call recordings into a compounding asset. It reads what objections actually came up and which responses preceded a won deal · so the rebuttals are evidence-based, not invented. Feeds straight into Cold-Call Scripting and Objection Response.

nodes.label: Demo Prototyping
nodes.description: Turn discovery notes into a working visual prototype before the next meeting.

playbook.human: AI builds the prototype; the human decides whether it ships. Nothing reaches a prospect without the seller’s eyes on it.
playbook.replaces: The two-week proposal gap where deals go cold. A visual prototype sent same-day collapses the “is this possible?” conversation entirely.

ladder.manual: A follow-up deck, eventually.
ladder.assisted: Discovery notes → working visual prototype + send message, same day, human reviews before it goes out.
ladder.autonomous: Every discovery call triggers a prototype draft; the human picks which ones to polish and send.

playbook.notes: Sell the dream: show them their end state before the proposal exists. The follow-up call stops being “convince me” and becomes “scope it.” The skill below extracts the brief from a transcript, picks the right format, and drafts the send message.

nodes.label: Proposal Generation
nodes.description: Generate branded proposals rendered to PDF from call context.

playbook.human: AI drafts structure and prose; a human owns scope and price on every proposal. Those two numbers are never delegated.
playbook.replaces: 3–6 hours per proposal · and for services firms doing tenders, often 2–3 days per response. This is frequently the bottleneck on revenue itself.

ladder.manual: Last proposal, find-and-replace, new logo.
ladder.assisted: Call context → drafted proposal in the house template, rendered to branded PDF; human edits scope and price.
ladder.autonomous: Proposal drafts generate from the deal record the moment a deal hits “proposal” stage, matched to the closest past win.

playbook.notes: Template matching is the unlock: your best past proposals become the pattern library. Build the brand template once, render programmatically forever. Architecture and professional-services firms run entire bid teams on what this node replaces.

nodes.label: Deal Room Assembly
nodes.description: Spin up tracked, password-gated deal rooms per prospect.

playbook.replaces: PDF proposals that get forwarded into the void. A tracked room tells you who opened what, when · intel a PDF can never give you.

ladder.manual: Attachment in an email thread.
ladder.assisted: Branded, password-gated room per prospect · proposal, scope, proof, pricing · spun up from a template.
ladder.autonomous: Rooms generate per deal with engagement tracking feeding the pipeline: you know which stakeholder read pricing twice.

playbook.notes: The forward-ability is the point · your champion sells internally with a link, not an attachment. Magic links per stakeholder turn open-data into a stakeholder map.

nodes.label: Agreement Drafting
nodes.description: Produce the services agreement the moment a deal closes verbally.

playbook.human: A lawyer blesses the master template once; a human reviews every generated agreement before it goes out. AI fills and adapts · it never invents a clause.
playbook.replaces: The 3–10 day gap between “yes” and paperwork, where verbal closes go to die. Plus $300–800 of lawyer time per agreement if you draft each one fresh instead of templating once.

ladder.manual: You hunt for the last client’s contract, find-and-replace their name, and miss one instance of it in clause 9.
ladder.assisted: The moment a deal closes verbally, the agreement generates from the deal record · parties, scope, fees, terms · into the lawyer-approved template, ready for human review and signature.
ladder.autonomous: Stage change to closed-won triggers the agreement, routes it for e-signature, and chases the unsigned · the human only touches deals with non-standard terms.

playbook.notes: Send the agreement the same day as the verbal yes · momentum is a closing tool and every day of silence invites second thoughts. Get one lawyer pass on the master template, then never freelance the legal language again; the AI’s job is filling variables, not writing clauses. The trap is letting per-deal “small tweaks” fork the template until no two contracts match.

nodes.label: Pricing Support
nodes.description: Model anchors, phase structures, and ROI comparisons per deal.

playbook.human: AI models the structures; the human picks the number. Price is positioning, leverage, and read-of-the-room · the final figure on every deal is a human call, never a model output.
playbook.replaces: Pricing by gut and anchoring low under pressure. The hour of FTE-comparison math and phase-structuring that justifies a 2–3× higher number · done properly for big deals, skipped for the rest.

ladder.manual: You pick a number on the call, feel it wobble, and discount before anyone asked you to.
ladder.assisted: Per deal: anchor comparisons, phase structures, and ROI math modeled from the discovery context · three defensible options with the reasoning attached, before the pricing conversation.
ladder.autonomous: Every deal entering proposal stage arrives with its pricing model pre-built · comparable past deals, suggested anchor, phase breakdown · and the human chooses rather than calculates.

playbook.notes: Anchor against the cost of the alternative, not your own effort · the comparison to a salary, an agency retainer, or the cost of the problem persisting is what makes a number feel small. Phase the structure so the first yes is easy and the relationship prices the rest. The trap is letting the model’s mid-range option become a ceiling; the math exists to defend ambition, not cap it.

nodes.label: CRM Hygiene
nodes.description: Keep records deduped, fields normalized, stages honest.

playbook.replaces: The 10–20% of records that are duplicates, dead, or wrong · and every report, forecast, and automation silently built on top of them. Garbage hygiene taxes every node downstream.

ladder.manual: Three records for the same company, a deal marked “proposal” since March, and nobody trusts the dashboard.
ladder.assisted: Dedupe candidates, stale stages, and missing fields surface on a schedule with proposed fixes; a human approves the merge.
ladder.autonomous: Records dedupe and normalize continuously, stages age out with prompts to the owner, and every new entry conforms on arrival · the CRM stays true without a cleanup day.

playbook.notes: Hygiene is the unglamorous prerequisite for the entire Pipeline Ops branch · reporting, forecasting, and reactivation all read from these records, and they inherit every error. Define “honest stage” rules in writing (what evidence moves a deal forward) and let the system enforce them. The trap is the quarterly cleanup blitz: hygiene is a standing process, not an event, and a CRM cleaned once decays in weeks.

nodes.label: Pipeline Reporting
nodes.description: Weekly pipeline state · what moved, what stalled, what closes next.

playbook.replaces: The Monday hour of assembling pipeline state by hand · or the more common alternative, running the business on whatever the founder remembers the pipeline looking like.

ladder.manual: Someone scrolls the CRM before the meeting and narrates it from memory.
ladder.assisted: A weekly digest lands on schedule: what moved, what stalled, what closes next, and which deals went quiet · with the deltas, not just the totals.
ladder.autonomous: The report writes and distributes itself, flags anomalies between editions, and answers ad-hoc pipeline questions on demand · the meeting reads the report instead of building it.

playbook.notes: Report movement, not state · “what changed since last week” is the entire value, and a static pipeline snapshot is just a screenshot with ceremony. Include a stalled-deals section with days-since-last-touch; it is the report’s most actionable line. The trap is metric sprawl: one page, same format weekly, so deviations jump out instead of hiding in noise.

nodes.label: Forecasting
nodes.description: Probability-weight the pipeline into a revenue forecast.

playbook.human: The model weights the pipeline; the deal owner adjusts the calls. A human who just left the room knows things no stage-probability ever will · the forecast is a draft until someone accountable signs it.
playbook.replaces: Revenue surprises in both directions. The founder’s number is usually hope-weighted, not probability-weighted · and the gap between them is the months of runway you didn’t know you were missing.

ladder.manual: You add up the pipeline, multiply by optimism, and call it a forecast.
ladder.assisted: Deals probability-weighted by stage, age, and engagement signals into a monthly revenue forecast · with the assumptions visible, so a human can argue with them.
ladder.autonomous: The forecast updates as deals move, learns from its own misses, and flags the gap between the model’s number and the owner’s · which is usually where the truth lives.

playbook.notes: Track forecast-versus-actual from day one · the model earns trust by being auditable, and three months of scorekeeping beats any methodology debate. Weight on behavior (engagement, momentum, days-in-stage) more than on stage labels, which mostly record what the seller hoped. The trap is false precision: a forecast with a range and visible assumptions is useful; a single confident number is theater.

nodes.label: Reactivation
nodes.description: Revive dormant deals and win back lost ones on a schedule.

playbook.human: A human approves the revival list monthly · some dead deals should stay dead, and only a human knows which.
playbook.replaces: The revenue sitting in your dead-deals column. Most pipelines have 6 figures of “went quiet” that nobody systematically revisits.

ladder.manual: You remember an old prospect in the shower.
ladder.assisted: Dormant deals surface on a schedule with a drafted, context-aware re-opener · referencing where things left off, leading with something new.
ladder.autonomous: Every deal that goes quiet enters a patient, spaced revival track automatically; replies route back to the pipeline.

playbook.notes: The re-opener must contain new value · a relevant build, a result in their vertical, a changed offer. “Just checking in” is not reactivation, it’s noise. Cheapest pipeline you’ll ever generate; the leads are already paid for.

nodes.label: Win/Loss Analysis
nodes.description: Tag why deals close or die; feed patterns back into targeting.

playbook.human: The losing seller writes the first draft of why · then someone who wasn’t in the deal reads it skeptically. Self-reported loss reasons are where pipelines lie to themselves most fluently.
playbook.replaces: Paying full tuition for every lost deal and keeping none of the lesson. Most teams can’t say why their last five losses died beyond “price” · which is almost never the real reason.

ladder.manual: A shrug, a “they went another direction”, and the same mistake next quarter.
ladder.assisted: Every closed deal gets tagged with a structured reason, drawn from the transcripts and thread history rather than the seller’s memory; patterns compile quarterly.
ladder.autonomous: Loss patterns surface as they form · a vertical going cold, an objection trending up, a competitor winning on the same line · and feed straight back into targeting and the objection library.

playbook.notes: The taxonomy is the build: eight to twelve fixed reasons, forced choice, free text optional · uncategorized losses are unanalyzable losses. Mine the call transcripts, not the seller’s recollection; the real reason is usually said out loud somewhere in the second call. The trap is collecting tags and never closing the loop · the analysis only pays when it changes the ICP, the pitch, or the price.

nodes.label: Marketing
nodes.subtitle: content · brand · distribution
nodes.description: The engine that makes you known · reading what works, making more of it, and pushing one good idea across every surface before the trend moves. Most teams post and pray. This department measures every piece against the median, doubles down on the winners, and turns a single reel into nine assets · so output stops depending on whoever felt inspired that week.

nodes.label: Performance Mining
nodes.description: Rank your own content corpus · what worked, what to re-hash.

playbook.replaces: Posting on instinct while your own corpus already knows what works. Your top 10 posts are a content strategy · if anything reads them.

ladder.manual: Scrolling your own profile for ideas.
ladder.assisted: The corpus ranked by performance, patterns extracted · hooks, formats, topics · with re-hash candidates flagged.
ladder.autonomous: Every new post is scored against the pattern library before it ships; winners auto-feed the idea queue.

playbook.notes: Re-hashing beats inventing: a proven idea in a new format outperforms a new idea in any format, and audiences forget faster than creators think.

nodes.label: Trend Monitoring
nodes.description: Watch the niche for breaking topics and rising formats.

playbook.replaces: An hour a day of feed-scrolling disguised as research.

ladder.manual: Whatever the algorithm showed you at breakfast.
ladder.assisted: Daily sweep of the niche · breaking topics, rising formats · distilled into content angles in your voice.
ladder.autonomous: The day’s angles land each morning, pre-matched to your pillars and ranked by fit.

playbook.notes: The skill below runs topic → articles → hooks → ready-to-draft ideas as one chain. Speed matters more than polish on trend content · the half-life is measured in days.

nodes.label: Competitor Analysis
nodes.description: Scrape and transcribe competitor content; extract hook patterns.

playbook.replaces: Watching competitors casually instead of systematically. Their viral posts are free R&D · someone else paid the testing cost.

ladder.manual: You saw their reel and felt something.
ladder.assisted: Competitor content scraped and transcribed; hook patterns, formats, and cadence extracted into a playbook.
ladder.autonomous: Watched accounts feed a standing pattern library; your hook generator consumes it directly.

playbook.notes: Transcription is the trick · the spoken hook is where the pattern lives, not the caption. Two skills below: one for Instagram reels, one for TikTok.

nodes.label: Audience Analysis
nodes.description: Mine comments and DMs for questions, objections, and content ideas.

playbook.replaces: Reading comments for dopamine instead of data. Your audience tells you exactly what to make next, every day, in writing · and almost nobody logs it.

ladder.manual: You vaguely remember someone asked about pricing once.
ladder.assisted: Comments and DMs mined on a schedule · questions, objections, and recurring pain extracted into a ranked content-idea queue.
ladder.autonomous: Every comment and DM feeds a standing demand map; new objections route to the idea queue and the offer doc without anyone scrolling.

playbook.notes: Objections are the gold · a question asked three times in comments is a reel, a guide, and an email in one. Pipe the output into Hook Writing so demand drives creation, not the other way around. The trap is mining only your winners: the comments on mediocre posts tell you why they were mediocre.

nodes.label: Hook Writing
nodes.description: Generate and rank hooks per platform from proven patterns.

playbook.replaces: The blank-page tax on every piece of content. The hook is 80% of performance and the part most creators spend the least time on.

ladder.manual: First line that comes to mind, posted.
ladder.assisted: 15–20 ranked hooks per idea, per platform, generated from proven patterns · you pick, you post.
ladder.autonomous: Every idea in the queue arrives with its hook variants attached; performance data re-ranks patterns monthly.

playbook.notes: Volume is the method: write twenty, ship one. The skill below generates per-platform · a LinkedIn hook and a TikTok hook are different species.

nodes.label: Script Writing
nodes.description: Full reel and video scripts in the house voice.

playbook.replaces: 2–3 hours per script done properly, or $150–500 per script from a freelancer who doesn’t sound like you. At a daily posting cadence that’s a part-time hire.

ladder.manual: You wing it to camera and hope take four has an ending.
ladder.assisted: Full scripts drafted in the house voice from a hook and an angle · structure, beats, CTA · human edits before filming.
ladder.autonomous: Every idea in the queue arrives scripted in two or three variations; performance data tunes the structure monthly.

playbook.notes: The voice file is the whole build · feed it real transcripts of your best-performing content, not your written posts, because spoken voice and written voice are different animals. Structure beats inspiration: hook → tension → payoff → CTA, every time. The trap is scripts that read well and speak badly · read every draft out loud before it’s approved.

nodes.label: Caption Writing
nodes.description: Platform-correct captions with CTA placement rules baked in.

playbook.replaces: The 20 minutes per post that happens after the creative energy is spent · which is why most captions are an afterthought stapled to good content.

ladder.manual: Emoji, three hashtags, post, regret.
ladder.assisted: Platform-correct captions drafted per asset · CTA placement, hashtag limits, and line-break rules baked in · human approves.
ladder.autonomous: Every queued post carries its caption variants; the rules update themselves as platforms change what works.

playbook.notes: Encode the platform rules once as hard constraints · where the CTA sits, how many hashtags, how the first line truncates in feed · and the agent never violates them at 11pm the way a tired human does. The first line is a second hook: it shows before the tap. The trap is one caption pasted everywhere; a LinkedIn caption and a TikTok caption share an idea, not a structure.

nodes.label: Carousel Production
nodes.description: Design and export branded carousel slides.

playbook.replaces: $100–300 per carousel from a designer with a 3-day turnaround, or 2–4 hours of founder time per set fighting a drag-and-drop tool.

ladder.manual: Canva, ten slides, fonts drifting by slide six.
ladder.assisted: Slides generated from a locked design system · copy in, branded PNGs out · human reviews the set before export.
ladder.autonomous: Winning ideas trigger carousel drafts automatically; the export pipeline renders and queues them for publishing.

playbook.notes: Build the design system once as code · templates, type scale, spacing, logo placement · then every carousel is a content problem, not a design problem. Slide one is a hook with the same stakes as a video hook; slides two through six earn the swipe one at a time. The trap is redesigning per carousel: lock the system and let consistency become the brand.

nodes.label: Video Production
nodes.description: Programmatic video · overlays, captions, motion graphics on recordings.

playbook.replaces: $50–150 per reel to an editor with a 2–5 day turnaround · and the turnaround is the real cost, because trend content dies waiting in someone’s queue.

ladder.manual: You learn a video editor’s timeline at midnight, once, badly.
ladder.assisted: Recordings get overlays, captions, and motion graphics applied programmatically from a reusable component library; human reviews the render.
ladder.autonomous: Drop a recording in a folder and a finished, captioned, on-brand edit comes out · variants included, queued for review.

playbook.notes: Programmatic video means edits defined in code, which means every solved problem · caption styling, transitions, overlay timing · becomes a reusable primitive instead of a memory. Build the primitives library first; the second video costs a tenth of the first. The trap is treating each video as a fresh project: copy the last working template, always.

nodes.label: Image Generation
nodes.description: Brand-consistent images from reference libraries.

playbook.replaces: Stock photos that look like stock photos, or $50–200/image from a designer for routine brand visuals.

ladder.manual: Canva at 11pm.
ladder.assisted: Brand-consistent images generated from a reference library · your visual language, learned and reproduced.
ladder.autonomous: Every post in the queue gets on-brand visual options generated alongside the copy.

playbook.notes: The reference library is the moat: feed it your best existing visuals and identity shots so output stays unmistakably yours. Two skills below · brand imagery and consistent-character personal imagery.

nodes.label: Thumbnail & Cover Design
nodes.description: Scroll-stopping thumbnails and covers tuned to earn the click.

playbook.replaces: The click you lose before anyone reads a word · most content dies on a weak thumbnail, not weak content.

ladder.manual: You slap a frame from the video on it and hope.
ladder.assisted: The agent generates thumbnail and cover variants tuned to the hook, in brand, ready to A/B.
ladder.autonomous: Covers generate per post from the hook, with the winning patterns fed back from performance data.

playbook.notes: The thumbnail is the ad for the content. The skill below produces scroll-stopping, on-brand covers and tests variants · pair it with Performance Mining so the winners teach the next batch.

nodes.label: Ad Creative
nodes.description: Generate and iterate paid-ad variations · hooks, angles, formats.

playbook.replaces: The creative bottleneck on every paid account · one ad, no variations, fatiguing while you sleep.

ladder.manual: A designer makes one ad a week; nothing gets tested.
ladder.assisted: The agent generates hook, angle, and format variations off your winners · ready to launch as a test batch.
ladder.autonomous: Fresh creative is generated and queued continuously, rotating before fatigue sets in, learning from spend.

playbook.notes: Paid acquisition is won on creative volume, not bid tweaks. The skill below spins winning ads into new angles and formats · the same engine behind the Meta Ads dashboard’s creative-fatigue flags.

nodes.label: Landing Page Copy
nodes.description: Conversion copy for the whole page · hero, proof, offer, FAQ, CTA.

playbook.replaces: A $2–5k copywriter per page, or worse · the founder writing feature lists nobody converts on.

ladder.manual: You write the page yourself, lead with features, and wonder why it doesn’t convert.
ladder.assisted: The agent writes the full page in the proven order · hero promise, problem, mechanism, proof, offer, FAQ, CTA · in your voice.
ladder.autonomous: Pages generate per offer and per campaign, with variants written for testing.

playbook.notes: Conversion copy is a structure, not a talent · hook, problem in their words, mechanism, proof, offer with risk reversal, objection FAQ, one CTA. The skill below writes the whole page section by section from your offer and ICP.

nodes.label: Deck Production
nodes.description: Webinar and talk decks in the brand design system.

playbook.replaces: 6–10 hours per webinar deck, or $500–1,500 to a designer who needs the content anyway · meaning you do the thinking twice.

ladder.manual: Last quarter’s deck with new dates and one new chart.
ladder.assisted: Talk outline in, branded deck out · house design system, real assets, consistent typography · human edits the narrative.
ladder.autonomous: Every booked talk or webinar triggers a deck draft from the topic and the knowledge base; you walk in and rehearse instead of build.

playbook.notes: Lock three or four master slide patterns · cover, content, proof, CTA · and every deck becomes assembly, not design. The deck is a sales asset wearing an education costume: proof slides and the close deserve the most iterations. The trap is template drift · one deck built off-system and every deck after it inherits the mutation.

nodes.label: Cross-Platform Adaptation
nodes.description: One idea → native formats for every platform.

playbook.replaces: The 5× content multiplier everyone talks about and almost nobody operationalizes, because manual repurposing is genuinely tedious.

ladder.manual: Same caption pasted to four apps.
ladder.assisted: One idea → native formats for every platform: LinkedIn post, X thread, newsletter section, video script, short-form scripts.
ladder.autonomous: Every flagship piece automatically fans out to the full format set, queued for review.

playbook.notes: Native beats syndicated · each platform gets its own structure, not a resize. The skill below runs one idea through research and out to seven formats.

nodes.label: Clip Extraction
nodes.description: Cut long recordings into short-form clips worth posting.

playbook.replaces: $1–2k/month clipping agencies, or an editor billing hours to watch footage. A one-hour webinar holds 5–10 postable clips that mostly die unwatched in a recordings folder.

ladder.manual: You meant to clip the webinar. That was three webinars ago.
ladder.assisted: Long recordings transcribed and scanned for standalone moments · strong claims, stories, answers · cut and captioned for review.
ladder.autonomous: Every long recording that lands triggers extraction; ranked clips arrive captioned and queued, no one asked.

playbook.notes: Select from the transcript, not the timeline · reading an hour takes four minutes, watching it takes an hour. A clip earns posting only if it works with zero context: a complete claim, a complete story, or a complete answer. The trap is volume worship · ten mediocre clips from one recording trains the audience to skip you; ship the two that stand alone.

nodes.label: Lead-Magnet Builds
nodes.description: Turn content themes into gated guides and landing pages.

playbook.replaces: The “we should make a guide” task that stays on the roadmap for two quarters.

ladder.manual: A PDF made once, promoted twice, forgotten.
ladder.assisted: Content themes that already performed become gated guides with landing pages, built end-to-end in a session.
ladder.autonomous: Top-performing topics trigger draft lead magnets automatically; the comment-CTA layer delivers them.

playbook.notes: Build magnets from proven demand only · the reel that popped tells you exactly what people want gated. Wire delivery to Comment-CTA Fulfillment in the Deals tree and the loop closes itself.

nodes.label: Publishing
nodes.description: Schedule and post across platforms via API.

playbook.human: A human eyeballs account, caption, and asset before each scheduled batch goes live. A wrong-account post is a screenshot forever · the two-minute check is non-negotiable.
playbook.replaces: The daily posting chore that survives exactly until the first busy week. Inconsistency is the silent killer of every content flywheel · the algorithm forgets faster than you recover.

ladder.manual: Phone out, app open, paste, post, repeat per platform · when you remember.
ladder.assisted: Approved content scheduled and posted across platforms via API; the queue shows what ships when, and gaps get flagged.
ladder.autonomous: The pipeline runs creation → caption → queue → post on cadence; a human curates the queue, the system never misses a day.

playbook.notes: Post via API, not via browser automation · platform APIs are the stable path and the account-safe one. Build the queue with a visible runway: knowing you have nine days of approved content banked changes how you create. The trap is going full autopilot on day one; run queue-plus-approval for a month before you let anything ship unseen.

nodes.label: Newsletter & Broadcast
nodes.description: Design and send the weekly email in the brand system.

playbook.replaces: 3–5 hours/week of writing and formatting, or $500–1k/month to a ghostwriter · and the issue that quietly skips a week, then two, then the list goes cold.

ladder.manual: Sunday night, blank editor, “what happened this week?”
ladder.assisted: The week’s content and wins harvested into a designed issue in the brand template · human edits the takes, hits send.
ladder.autonomous: The issue assembles itself on schedule from the week’s shipped work; you review Thursday, it sends Friday, every week, forever.

playbook.notes: Build the HTML template once in the brand system and never design an issue again · the weekly job becomes pure editorial. Harvest, don’t write: the newsletter should be assembled from content and work that already exists, with one original take on top. The trap is treating it as a broadcast instead of an asset · the list is the only audience you own; everything else is rented.

nodes.label: SEO & GEO
nodes.description: Make the site legible to search engines and LLMs.

playbook.replaces: $1–3k/month SEO retainers that mostly produce reports · or being invisible to the growing share of buyers who ask an LLM for a recommendation instead of searching.

ladder.manual: Someone installed an SEO plugin in 2023 and the site has been “optimized” ever since.
ladder.assisted: Sitemap, structured data, metadata, and an llms.txt generated and maintained from the actual site content; gaps audited on demand.
ladder.autonomous: Every new page ships pre-optimized for both crawlers and LLMs; rankings and AI-citation checks run on schedule and flag drift.

playbook.notes: GEO · being legible and citable to LLMs · is the part most sites have done nothing about, and it is mostly the same hygiene as SEO done properly: clear structure, structured data, plain statements of what you do and for whom. Do the foundation pass in one session: sitemap, robots, schema markup, llms.txt. The trap is chasing keywords before fixing legibility · a site a machine can’t parse loses on every query, optimized or not.

nodes.label: OG & Share Surface
nodes.description: Every page ships with share-ready open-graph imagery.

playbook.replaces: Links that unfurl as a blank gray rectangle in every DM, Slack, and LinkedIn share. Each naked link is a small credibility tax, paid on the exact surface where your content travels.

ladder.manual: One static og-image uploaded at launch, wrong dimensions, never updated.
ladder.assisted: A templated OG image per page type · title pulled in, brand system applied · generated at build time.
ladder.autonomous: Every page and post ships with its share card rendered automatically; new routes inherit the system with zero extra work.

playbook.notes: Generate OG images programmatically from a template route, not as design files · the title, page type, and brand frame compose at request time and new content is covered forever. Test the unfurl where it actually happens: a messaging app, a LinkedIn draft, an X compose box. The trap is one generic image site-wide; per-page cards with the real title get measurably more clicks because they read as content, not as a logo.

nodes.label: Deal Scripting
nodes.description: Sponsored scripts in the proven format, per brand brief.

playbook.human: Two approvals, both human: the sponsor signs off on claims, and the creator approves every line spoken under their name. Never let an agent invent a capability claim for someone else’s product · fact-check before it goes on camera.
playbook.replaces: Days of back-and-forth per sponsored script, with revision cycles quietly eating the deal’s margin. A $5k brand deal at four revision rounds is a $2k brand deal.

ladder.manual: The brand sends a brief; you procrastinate, then write something neither of you loves.
ladder.assisted: Brief in, three script variations out · proven format, real product claims checked, creator voice intact · sponsor picks one.
ladder.autonomous: Signed deals trigger scripted variations automatically from the brief plus your top-performing formats; humans handle approval, not drafting.

playbook.notes: Send three variations, not one · sponsors who choose between options approve faster than sponsors asked to judge a single take. Anchor every script in a format your own data says works; the brand bought your audience, and your audience came for your format. The trap is letting the brief flatten the voice · a sponsored post that sounds like an ad performs like an ad, which serves nobody who paid for it.

nodes.label: Approval Docs
nodes.description: Brand-safe formatted docs for sponsor sign-off.

playbook.replaces: Script versions scattered across email threads and chat, plus 30–60 minutes per deal of formatting · multiplied by every revision round the mess itself creates.

ladder.manual: Version 3 is in email, version 4 is in WhatsApp, the brand approved version 2.
ladder.assisted: The locked script lands in a clean, brand-safe formatted doc · consistent naming, proper structure · ready for sponsor sign-off.
ladder.autonomous: Final scripts generate their approval doc automatically, filed per brand, shared with minimum-scope access; revisions update one canonical document.

playbook.notes: One canonical doc per deal, edits in the doc, never in chat · the entire job is killing version ambiguity. A consistent naming convention and a clean format do quiet sales work too: sponsors judge professionalism from the artifacts, and tidy paperwork earns the second deal. The trap is over-sharing · scope access to the single file, not your whole drive.

nodes.label: Operations
nodes.subtitle: onboarding · builds · client ops
nodes.description: Where promises become delivery · onboarding a new client, wiring the systems, testing the work, and reporting status before anyone has to ask. Delivery dies in week one or it doesn’t. This department makes the first week feel like the tenth, catches the broken batch before the client sees it, and sends the Friday update that keeps trust alive through the quiet stretches.

nodes.label: Kickoff Pack
nodes.description: Welcome email, access checklist, and project scaffold the day a deal closes.

playbook.replaces: The 3–5 day dead zone between signature and first real work · the window where buyer’s remorse lives. Plus 2–3 hours of assembling the same welcome email, checklist, and folder structure for every new client.

ladder.manual: The client signs, then hears nothing until someone finds a spare afternoon.
ladder.assisted: Deal closes → welcome email, access checklist, and project folder drafted from the deal record; the delivery lead reviews and sends same-day.
ladder.autonomous: The signed agreement triggers the full pack automatically · email out, checklist live, scaffold built · before the celebratory Slack message.

playbook.notes: Speed here sets the tone for the whole engagement: a kickoff pack landing within hours of signing tells the client they bought from operators. Template the pack once · welcome email, what-happens-next timeline, access checklist · and personalize from the deal record, not from scratch. The trap is over-stuffing it: one email, one checklist, one clear next step. Anything more gets ignored.
playbook.human: The delivery lead sends the welcome email under their own name and owns the kickoff date it promises. The pack assembles itself; the commitment is human.

nodes.label: Access Collection
nodes.description: Chase and verify every credential and API key needed to build.

playbook.replaces: The 1–2 weeks of “still waiting on that API key” that delays every build start · the single most common cause of week-one slippage, and it bills nobody.

ladder.manual: You email asking for credentials, they send half, you notice the gap mid-build.
ladder.assisted: A checklist generated per project from the scoped stack; the agent chases outstanding items on a schedule and verifies each credential actually works on receipt.
ladder.autonomous: Every received key is test-called immediately, gaps re-chased automatically, and the build gets a green light only when the full set verifies.

playbook.notes: Verification is the half everyone skips: a key that arrives is not a key that works · wrong scopes, expired tokens, and sandbox-only credentials surface mid-build if you don’t test on receipt. Derive the checklist from the actual scoped integrations, not a generic template. Trap to avoid: marking items complete when they arrive instead of when they verify.
playbook.human: Credentials are handled by a named human into a proper secrets store · never pasted into chat, never stored in the agent’s context. The agent chases and verifies; it does not hold the keys.

nodes.label: Project Scaffolding
nodes.description: Stand up the repo, context files, and plan for a new engagement.

playbook.replaces: The half-day of setup before any real work starts · repo, context files, folder conventions, plan doc · done slightly differently every time, so no two projects are navigable the same way.

ladder.manual: Every project starts as an empty folder and someone’s memory of how the last one was structured.
ladder.assisted: One command stands up the repo, client context file, plan doc, and folder conventions from the house template; a human fills in the engagement specifics.
ladder.autonomous: The closed deal triggers the scaffold automatically · pre-populated with everything the sales process already learned about the client.

playbook.notes: The real product here is consistency: when every engagement has the same skeleton, any agent or human can drop into any project and orient in one read. Pull the initial context from the deal record and discovery transcripts · the sales process already captured most of it; re-asking the client is an admission you don’t talk to yourself. Keep the template minimal: scaffolds that demand twenty files get abandoned by file six.

nodes.label: Document Extraction
nodes.description: High-volume structured extraction from client documents.

playbook.human: Humans review the low-confidence queue and own the gold-standard set. The machine earns autonomy field by field, measured against it.
playbook.replaces: Teams of people reading documents and retyping them into systems. At volume this is entire payrolls · the densest ROI node on this map for document-heavy businesses.

ladder.manual: Humans read, humans type, humans err.
ladder.assisted: Documents → structured fields via an extraction pipeline, with confidence scores and human review on the low-confidence tail.
ladder.autonomous: High-confidence extractions flow straight to the system of record; accuracy benchmarked continuously against a gold set.

playbook.notes: Benchmark before you celebrate: build a 50-document gold-standard set and measure field-level accuracy against it. The review-queue pattern (auto-accept above threshold, human below) gets you production-safe long before the model is perfect. Probation services, insurance, compliance · whole verticals run on this node.

nodes.label: Integration Builds
nodes.description: Wire client systems together · CRMs, calendars, transcripts, payments.

playbook.replaces: The core billable work of an automation practice · and the part where scope creeps silently. Done by hand, each integration is days of reading API docs, handling auth, and discovering the vendor’s documentation lied.

ladder.manual: A developer reads the API docs, writes the glue, and finds the undocumented rate limit in production.
ladder.assisted: The agent writes the integration · auth, endpoints, error handling, retries · against verified credentials; a human reviews the code and runs it against real data.
ladder.autonomous: Standard integrations (CRM, calendar, transcripts, payments) assemble from a proven pattern library; humans only touch the genuinely novel ones.

playbook.notes: Build the pattern library deliberately: every integration you ship becomes a reusable template, and by the tenth project most builds are assembly, not invention. Always build against the client’s real data early · sandbox data hides the edge cases that blow up demos. The trap is skipping retry and failure handling because the happy path worked: integrations don’t fail in testing, they fail at 2am on day forty.

nodes.label: Data Migration
nodes.description: Move and clean data between systems without losing or mangling a row.

playbook.replaces: The migration project that quotes at $5–20k and still loses rows · or the intern hand-copying records between two CRMs for a fortnight.

ladder.manual: Someone exports a CSV, maps columns by hand, re-imports, and prays nothing broke.
ladder.assisted: The agent maps the fields, transforms, dedupes, validates row counts both sides, and reports exactly what moved and what didn’t.
ladder.autonomous: Ongoing syncs run on a schedule with reconciliation checks · drift gets flagged before it compounds.

playbook.notes: Migrations fail silently · a thousand rows in, nine hundred out, and nobody notices until a client does. The skill below maps, transforms, and reconciles with row-count validation so "did we lose anything" is answerable, not hoped.

nodes.label: Portal Provisioning
nodes.description: Spin up client-scoped delivery portals with live status.

playbook.replaces: The “can you send me an update?” email and the status deck rebuilt before every check-in call · 2–3 hours/week per active client of pure performance theatre.

ladder.manual: Status lives in email threads and whatever the client remembers from the last call.
